title: Edebiyatın yükselen yıldızı: TOLGA ÖZDOĞAN
desc: Fuarcılık sektöründeki yöneticilik kariyerini edebiyat dünyasındaki derin gözlemleriyle harmanlayan yazar Tolga Özdoğan ile yazarlık serüveni ve 'Leyla - Yasak Mevsim' üzerine çok özel bir söyleşi.
content:
- Sizi yakından tanıyabilir miyiz?

Ben Tolga Özdoğan. 1985 yılının Nisan ayında doğdum ve havasıyla, suyuyla, ritmiyle ruhuma en çok hitap eden şehirde, İzmir’de yaşıyorum. Profesyonel hayatımda fuarcılık sektöründe görev yapıyorum; aynı zamanda 20 yıla aşkın sektöre emek veren eski bir gazeteciyim. Fuarcılık gibi son derece dinamik, insan odaklı ve tempolu bir sektörde yöneticilik yaparken, gazeteci kimliğim dünyayı görsel bir estetikle algılamamı sağlıyor. Ancak tüm bu unvanların ötesinde, hayatımdaki en sarsılmaz kimliklerim; eşim Sevim’e duyduğum derin yol arkadaşlığı ve 2017 doğumlu oğlumuz Ege’nin babası olmamdır. Gündüzleri iş dünyasının o bitmek bilmeyen koşturmacasında kitleleri ağırlarken, geceleri kelimelerin o sessiz, yalıtılmış ve sonsuz evrenine sığınıyorum. Ben, kalabalıkların içindeki o yalnızlığı kelimelerle sağaltmaya çalışan biriyim.

- Yazarlığa adım atmanızdaki asıl kırılma noktası ne oldu?

İnsanın dünyadaki varoluşunu, kendi eliyle yarattığı o büyük kaosu ve ardından umutsuzca aradığı düzeni derinlemesine sorgulamaya başladığım dönemler en büyük eşikti. İş dünyasında ve toplumsal hayatta insanların kurduğu sistemleri, taktıkları maskeleri ve içlerindeki çelişkileri gözlemlemek bende bir tortu oluşturdu. Bu tortunun zihnimde birikip taşma noktasına gelmesi, o karmaşayı kâğıt üzerinde anlamlandırarak bir edebi düzene kavuşturma ihtiyacı doğurdu. Sadece gözlemlemek yetmemeye, o gözlemleri kalıcı bir forma dönüştürme arzusu ağır basmaya başladığında yazar olmanın kaçınılmaz olduğunu anladım.

- Sizi ilk kez kalemi elinize almaya iten özel bir an var mıydı?

Mekanik daktilolara duyduğum o tarifsiz tutku aslında bir tesadüf değildi. O tuşlara her bastığımda çıkan tok, ritmik ses, kâğıda işleyen o fiziksel güç, bana her zaman henüz anlatılmamış hikâyelerin kapısını araladı. O ses bir nevi geçmişin kalbi gibi atıyordu. Fakat kalemi elime temelli almamı ve bir eser bırakma güdüsünü tetikleyen asıl büyük patlama, oğlum Ege’nin dünyaya gelişidir. Bir insan yetiştirirken zamana karşı ne kadar aciz olduğunuzu fark ediyorsunuz. Ona, geleceğe ve dünyaya benden geriye kalacak en anlamlı izin, zamana direnen kelimeler olması gerektiğine inandığım o an, yazarlığa ilk ve en güçlü adımı attım.

- Çocukluğunuzdaki veya gençliğinizdeki okuma alışkanlıklarınızın bugünkü yazım dilinize ve üslubunuza nasıl bir etkisi oldu?

Okumak, zihnimin sınırlarını çok erken yaşta yıktı. Dostoyevski’nin Karamazov Kardeşler‘deki o emsalsiz psikolojik derinliği, insan ruhunun karanlık dehlizlerine inmekten korkmamayı öğretti bana. Gabriel García Márquez’in Yüzyıllık Yalnızlık‘ta ustalıkla kurduğu büyülü evren, hayal gücümün prangalarını kopardı. George Orwell’in 1984 ile yüzümüze çarptığı sistem eleştirisi ve distopik gerçeklik, toplumsal yapıları sorgulama biçimimi şekillendirdi. Buna Carl Sagan’ın o muazzam kozmik vizyonunu, Erich Maria Remarque’ın ve Theodore Dreiser’ın çarpıcı edebi dokunuşlarını da eklediğinizde, ortaya çok katmanlı bir altyapı çıkıyor. Tüm bu ustalardan süzülenler, üslubumda hem gerçekçi ve sert bir yüzleşmeyi hem de geniş bir düşünsel zemini aynı potada eritmemi sağladı.

- Hangi deneyimlerden sonra yazar olmaya karar verdiniz?

Yıllardır fuarcılık sektörünün tam kalbinde, uluslararası organizasyonları yönetiyorum. Bu iş bana binlerce insanla, farklı kültürlerle ve yüzlerce farklı dinamikle temas etme şansı veriyor. Bir gazeteci ve tasarımcı olarak görsel bir düzen yaratmaya çalışırken, bir yandan da insanın o kusurlu, öngörülemez doğasına tanıklık ediyorum. İnsanların toplum içinde kurduğu suni sistemleri, hırslarını, yıktıkları kuralları yakından gözlemlemek, içimdeki anlatma arzusunu körükledi. Toplumsal çelişkilerimizi ve bireyin kendi içindeki o bitmek bilmeyen denge arayışını izlemek, beni tüm bu kaotik deneyimleri felsefi ve edebi bir süzgeçten geçirmeye mecbur bıraktı.

- İyi bir yazar olmanın şartları nelerdir siz bu yolda nasıl bir yöntem izlediniz?

İyi bir yazar her şeyden önce yargılamadan, sadece “anlamak” için bakabilen keskin bir gözlemci olmalıdır. Dünyaya bir yargıç gibi değil, bir kâşif gibi yaklaşmalıdır. Ben bu yolda acele etmemeyi, kelimelerin içimde demlenmesine zaman tanımayı seçtim. Bazen bir cep saatinin kusursuz mekaniğini incelerken, bazen de evimdeki tatlı su akvaryumunda süzülen melek balıklarının o telaşsız ritmine bakarken yakaladığım o sessiz detayları, metinlerimin kalbine yerleştirmeye çalıştım. Disiplin ve hayatın akışındaki o gizli ahengi yakalayabilmek, benim temel yöntemim oldu.

- Kaleme aldığınız ilk kitap nedir ve varsa diğer kitaplarınız nelerdir?

Yazım hayatım, insanın kendi varoluşunu ve sistemle olan mücadelesini kurgu dışı bir düzlemde, felsefi bir derinlikle incelediğim Kaosun Mimarı İnsan ile başladı. Ardından bu temanın tamamlayıcısı niteliğindeki Düzenin Savunucusu İnsan geldi. Kurgu dünyasında ise tabuları, insan doğasının zaaflarını ve kural tanımaz bir hikâyeyi anlattığım Leyla – Yasak Mevsim romanımı kaleme aldım.

- Kitaplarınızdaki konuları yazmaya yönlendiren en önemli etken ya da etkenler nelerdir?

En temel etken; insanın o zıtlıklarla dolu, öngörülemez doğasıdır. Bizler, kendi elimizle kusursuz diye inşa ettiğimiz sistemleri ve düzenleri, gün gelip kendi hırslarımızla bir kaosa çeviren; ardından o yarattığımız yıkıntılar arasında yeniden umutsuzca bir çıkış yolu arayan varlıklarız. Yıkma ve yapma dürtüleri arasındaki o ince çizgi, insanın kendi zihniyle girdiği o acımasız savaş, kalemimi yönlendiren en güçlü pusuladır. Ben, içimizdeki o bitmeyen fırtınaları deşifre etmek istiyorum.

- Hikâyeyi kurgularken karakterlerinizin kaderini önceden tamamen planlıyor musunuz, yoksa yazım sürecinde karakterlerin kendi yollarını çizdiği oluyor mu?

Masaya oturduğumda zihnimde elbette sağlam bir mimari iskelet oluyor. Ancak edebiyat matematiğe benzemiyor. Kelimeler kâğıda dökülmeye başladığında, özellikle de Leyla – Yasak Mevsim’in derinlerine inerken bunu iliklerime kadar hissettim; karakterler bir anda canlanıyor ve kendi nefeslerini almaya başlıyorlar. Sizin onlara bir tanrı gibi çizdiğiniz o dar sınırları aşıyor, kendi doğruları, yanlışları ve arzularıyla hikâyeyi bambaşka bir mecraya sürüklüyorlar. Yazarlık tam da bu noktada onlara hükmetmek değil, onların sesine saygı duyup yollarını açabilme erdemidir.

- Size ilham veren şeyler nelerdir?

İlham benim için büyük şatafatlarda değil, yaşanmışlıklarda ve detaylarda saklıdır. Tarihin ağırlığını taşıyan vintage bir obje; örneğin 1970’lerden kalma mekanik bir kol saati ya da eski bir porselen biblo, zihnimde o dönemin yaşanmışlıklarına dair yepyeni pencereler açabilir. Evimizin neşesi, Afrika gri papağanımız Paşa’nın zeki ve anlık bir tepkisi, bir canlının dünyayı nasıl algıladığına dair bana ilham verebilir. Kısacası hayatın içinde otantik olan, yaşanmışlık barındıran her detay kalemimi besliyor.

- En çok hangi dönemlerde üretken oluyorsunuz ve yazma konusunda sizi en çok motive eden şey nedir?

Gündüzün koşturmacası bitip de dünyanın sessizliğe büründüğü o derin gece saatlerinde kalemim özgürleşiyor. Beni en çok motive eden şey ise zamana direnen bir iz bırakmak; özellikle oğlum Ege’ye, babasının zihninden dökülen kelimelerle inşa edilmiş, hiçbir zaman yıkılmayacak edebi bir miras bırakma düşüncesi içimdeki en güçlü yakıt.

- Okuyucular neden sizin kitabınızı okumalı?

Okuyuculara hazır, süslü reçeteler sunmuyorum; onlara kendi içlerindeki kaosu gösterecek net bir ayna tutuyorum. Maskelerinden sıyrılıp, insan doğasının o çelişkili ama bir o kadar da büyüleyici gerçeğiyle yüzleşmek istiyorlarsa sayfalarımın arasında kendilerini bulacaklardır.

- Kitap ya da kitaplarınızdaki ana fikirler ve vermek istediğiniz mesajlar nelerdir?

İnsan zihninin yıkıcı ve yapıcı gücü arasındaki o bitmek bilmeyen savaş… En büyük savaş alanımız her zaman kendi içimizdir. Dünyayı değiştirmeye kalkışmadan önce, içimizdeki o kaosu anlamak, yüzleşmek ve kendi düzenimizi savunmak zorundayız.

- Yazar olmanın ve yazmanın sizin için zor yanları nelerdir, bunlarla nasıl başa çıktınız?

Fuarcılık sektörünün tam kalbinde, yöneticilik gibi yüksek tempolu ve insan odaklı bir görevi yürütürken edebi bir izolasyon sağlamak en büyük zorluk. Bu dengeyi, yazmayı bir sorumluluk veya iş olarak değil, ruhsal bir sığınak olarak görerek kuruyorum.

- Yazar tıkanıklığı yaşadığınızda bu durumun üstesinden nasıl geliyorsunuz?

Asla kelimelerle inatlaşmıyorum. Zihnim yorulduğunda dünyamı değiştiriyorum. Farklı ilgi alanlarıma odaklanıyorum. Aceleci davranmak ve aşırı endişeli olmak sizi bir tıkanıklığa itebiliyor. Tabi ki eşimin, oğlumun, ailemin ve dostlarımın destekleri de çok önemli.

- Kitaplarınızı kitlelere ulaştırmak için ne gibi organizasyonlar yapıyorsunuz?

Dijital dünyayı ve modern araçları iletişimde aktif kullanıyorum. Ancak asıl heyecanım, önümüzdeki Eylül ayında gerçekleştireceğimiz lansman ve imza günü. Kelimelerin kâğıttan taşıp okurla fiziksel olarak buluşacağı o an için sabırsızlanıyorum.

- Kitap fuarlarındaki okur-yazar buluşmalarının sizin için önemi nedir?

Yıllarını fuarcılık sektörüne vermiş biri olarak, yüz yüze iletişimin, o sinerjinin gücüne inanıyorum. Bir kitabın sayfalarından çıkıp, onu okuyan gözlerle doğrudan temas kurmak, yazarın ruhunu besleyen en büyük ödül. Fuarlar, edebiyatın ete kemiğe büründüğü gerçek şölenlerdir. Elbette bende kitap fuarlarında okuyucularımla buluşmayı arzu ediyorum ve bu yönde çalışmalar yapıyorum.

- Şu an üzerinde çalıştığınız yeni projeleriniz var mı?

Yazarlık kariyerime roman yazarı olarak devam etmeyi planlıyor ve arzu ediyorum. Takdir edersiniz ki bir romanı oluşturmak zaman ve emek isteyen bir iş. Üzerinde çalıştığım taslaklarım elbette var. Öncesinde gerçekten çok inandığım ve ilk göz ağrım dediğim Leyla Yasak Mevsim’i geniş kitleler ve edebiyat dünyası ile tam olarak buluşturmak istiyorum. Gönül rahatlığı ile söyleyebilirim ki önümüzdeki dönemde de okuyucularım ve edebiyat severlerin ilham alacağı eserleri yayınlamaya devam edeceğim.

- Sizi en çok duygulandıran geri dönüşler nelerdir?

Bir okurumun, satırlarımda kendi içsel savaşıyla yüzleşme cesaretini bulduğunu ve hayatındaki o kaosu düzene sokmak için ayağa kalktığını söylemesi… Bir yazar için kelimelerinin bir başkasının hayatına dokunmasından daha tatmin edici bir geri dönüş olamaz. Ayrıca yeni çıkan romanım için bir edebiyat yarışmasında aday gösterileceğini öğrenmek benim için eşsiz bir duyguydu.

- Yazar adaylarına ne gibi tavsiyelerde bulunmak istersiniz?

Sadece kendi türünüzde değil; bilimden tarihe, klasiklerden bilim kurguya kadar çok geniş bir yelpazede beslenin. Hemen yayımlama telaşına düşmeyin. Kelimelerin zihninizde kendi ağırlığını bulmasına izin verin. Benim yayınladığım eserlerim 4 yıllık bir çalışmanın ürünü. Gözlem yapın ama başkalarının ne dediğine kulak tıkayın. Dünyayı bir kâşif gibi izleyip, kendi sesinizi inşa edin. Unutmayın kelimeler sizin nefesiniz, kaleminiz ise sesinizdir.



Kaynak Bilgisi: Bu özel röportaj Edebiyat Gündemi için derlenmiştir.

title: The Dream of Homeownership Is Haunted by Eviction in This Debut Novel
desc: The premise of Andrea Uptmor’s debut novel,The New People, is both gloriously simple and fraught with tension. Newlyweds Emma and Rachel move into a recently foreclosed house in a Midwestern campus to...
content:
The premise of Andrea Uptmor’s debut novel,The New People, is both gloriously simple and fraught with tension. Newlyweds Emma and Rachel move into a recently foreclosed house in a Midwestern campus town in 2008, but unbeknownst to them, the evicted former owners Charlotte and Dirk are still living in the attic in a form of illicit cohabitation known as phrogging. The contested space of the house—which Charlotte begins to sabotage in the hopes that “the new people” will leave—ultimately grounds the novel’s larger questions about the domestic infrastructure of marriage, homeownership, and parenthood, especially for people whose access to those social institutions has been restricted.

As a queer millennial who experienced the travails of trying to secure the legal protections of marriage well before the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges ruling, I had no idea how much it would mean to me to encounter a story like this one. Uptmor’s insights into the pressures that both legal and social queerphobia exert on Emma and Rachel’s marriage is pitch-perfect, and I loved the unexpected way in which she intertwines their struggles with those of the much older straight couple. Her approach feels refreshingly nuanced and true to the lived complexities of navigating queer adulthood in a predominantly conservative community. The book frequently made me laugh, and even moved me to tears in public. I should also mention that it is built far more sturdily than the fictional house in question, with well-finished prose and an elegantly constructed plot. In short, it’s a novel I will be thrusting into the hands of queer and straight friends alike in the coming months.

In anticipation of the book’s release, Uptmor and I had a delightful conversation over Zoom this spring about living hauntings and contested domestic spaces, as well as the intersections of queer and economic issues that drew her to revisit 2008 with these particular characters.

Jules Fitz Gerald: I once heard Carmen Maria Machado speak about all stories being haunted house stories, in the sense that they’re haunted both by their writers and by their readers. If you think of yourself as a ghost, what prompted you to haunt this particular fictional house in Indiana?

Andrea Uptmor:This idea of illegally occupying somebody’s home has always been interesting to me. When my wife and I bought our first house in 2013 in South Minneapolis, it was in the middle of a huge rash of foreclosures in the neighborhood, and the day after we moved in, our neighbor was evicted due to foreclosure. Right after he left, a group of squatters moved in and occupied the house. Law enforcement was there all the time with their guns drawn, the windows were broken in, but they couldn’t get these people to leave. It was so fascinating to me, this idea that, for me, home ownership was about a mortgage, and for the people next door, it was about occupying a space. It wasn’t until I learned about phrogging, which is living in somebody’s house without their knowledge—sort of an actual living haunting—that I thought, oh, that’s the story. Because then you’ve got that automatic tension between the people who believe they own the house and the people who are occupying it.

The house becomes this microcosm of what’s happening in the country.

In terms of why Indiana, that’s a good question. I was living in Iowa at the time that I wrote this and was really feeling what Emma feels throughout the book—not quite belonging, being a woman married to a woman. Like Iowa, Indiana can be one of those on-the-fence places where you just never know, when someone’s cleaning your teeth at the dentist’s office, or giving you an Uber ride, whether they’re a safe person or not. I wanted to recreate that environment for Emma and [the] other characters where there’s this air of uncertainty, where you’re not always sure if people are being intentionally aggressive or bigoted or homophobic, or whether it’s being perceived through Emma’s conditioning.

JFG: I loved how you handled that in the book. I live very far from Indiana, in rural Oregon, but what you’re describing really resonates. Beyond the place, it was interesting as a reader to look back on that time period, especially as rights that once seemed like legal certainties–like marriage equality–are increasingly in question. What was it like for you to write 2008 from the vantage point of the present?

AU:I’m very nostalgic for 2008. I would love to go back right now and have eight years of Obama ahead of me. But it was a pretty grim time, economically speaking. Nearly 2.5 million homeowners lost their homes to foreclosure. There was high unemployment. People’s 401Ks were tanking. There was a huge recession. At the same time, there was this brief window in California where same sex marriage was legal . . . then Proposition Eight passed, and it was no longer legal. We look back on 2008 with this sense of nostalgia and hope now, but when you were living it in the moment, people were losing their jobs, their money, their marriages, their rights to marry. It felt like the domestic infrastructure of people’s lives was disappearing. And if I wanted to write a story where a post-retirement couple was willing to endure the discomfort and humiliation of phrogging in their own attic, 2008 is probably the most likely time that this could have actually happened. The house becomes this microcosm of what’s happening in the country. The people in the attic, Charlotte and Dirk, are dealing with money issues and with a child who [lives with] addiction and mental illness. And the people downstairs, Emma and Rachel, are navigating being a queer couple in a conservative area. They’re all in the same space, but they’re having these wildly different experiences. Yet when they’re placed together in a narrative, there’s a lot of overlap.

JFG: I really appreciated how the book is a portrait of these two different marriages at very different life stages. What led you to write Charlotte and Emma as dual narrators rather than, say, going back and forth between Emma and Rachel?

Quite a bit of the loss [in the book] is characters having to reconcile themselves to their lives going a different way than they’d expected.

AU:It’s fun to reflect on these things because a lot of times the writing is instinctive, or you just pick up a trail. Of the four main characters, if I was going to dedicate a couple years of my life to really thinking about them, Emma and Charlotte are the two I liked the most and wanted to spend the most time with. I started with Emma because her experience most closely aligns with mine, and I think that’s often a place where writers start. I had this idea in my head, like you said, of a portrait of these two marriages, but I originally thought of them as political or generational foils, where we’ve got the conservative folks in the attic, and the lesbians downstairs, and you know, what’s gonna happen? The nuance grew through the editing. As I wrote, I realized Charlotte is so much more complex than I had originally intended, and it’s reductionist to try to just boil her down. She’s obviously Republican, but that’s not really important to the story.



Kaynak Bilgisi: Bu uluslararası içerik Electric Lit Söyleşileri üzerinden derlenmiş ve eksiksiz olarak Türkçeye çevrilmiştir.

title: Migration Touches Every Life
desc: Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. InThe Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice fa...
content:
Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. InThe Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice factory in Mexico. InTell Me How It Ends, she listened to, transcribed, and interpreted the testimonies of undocumented children. InLost Children Archive, the protagonist is a sound documentarist. InEchoes from the Borderlands, Luiselli moved beyond the page to bring the US-Mexico border to life in a 24-hour sonic essay/chapbook that was originally presented as a sound installation. Her newest novel,Beginning Middle End, is written in fragments and includes the sounds of volcanoes exhaling and fishermen singing, among other recordings from Sicily accessible via a QR code in the book.

Beginning Middle Endis a mother-daughter road novel that journeys through time and genre. The story unfolds in vignettes as an unnamed narrator and her 12-year-old daughter travel to Sicily to return an archeological relic that the mother’s grandmother had taken years before when she migrated to Mexico. Interspersed polaroid pictures, postcards, and sounds become records of their lives, blurring the boundary of narrative forms as the novel dives into geography, mythology, and archeology. Yet, the beating heart of the story remains these four generations of women, all storytellers in their own way. The narrator/mother is writing her own novel about a mother and daughter on a journey; meanwhile, the daughter is documenting their trip through letters and photographs to her grandmother, whose memory is rapidly failing––archiving memories for the one who is losing them.

The result: a novel that folds time and writing itself. A tripartite novel with three suitcases, a title in three parts, and a fourth layer nestled inside, like the great-grandmother of the stolen relic and the memories the characters inBeginning Middle Endare trying to piece together. The story leaves the reader wondering how fractured memories can be preserved and told through fabricated narratives. What is it to live in themiddlewhen memories are fading away?

Valeria Luiselli and I are both Mexican writers, born on the same day of the same year, both living in the United States. Via Zoom, we talked about sounds, migration, tectonic plates, translation, and the power of fiction and narrative to shape children’s imaginations.

Ofelia Montelongo: As I was reading the novel, I kept thinking about how themes of displacement and the mother-daughter relationship have been central to your earlier work. How did your earlier work migrate into the imagination of this novel?

There’s always a moment in a novel when you have to abandon a path because you are already on another. Those abandoned paths are ones that I often pick up again in another book.

Valeria Luiselli:There is a line of continuity in many of my books. Maybe not a line that traverses all of them. I certainly see a very clear line fromLos ingrávidosorFaces in the Crowd(2011), through this tiny thing I wrote that very few people have read calledSwings of Harlem––a map of swings in Harlem where I started using Polaroid photography for the first time while documenting, in that case, a neighborhood and the swings in the neighborhood. And then, fromSwings Of HarlemtoLost Children Archiveand, of course,Tell Me How it Endsas well, but that’s a very straightforward, nonfictional testimonial piece.

OM: How are the narrators and main characters different in each story? And different from you as the author?

VL:The characters are not the same. The narrator has a different profession in each of the books. InLos Ingrávidosshe’s a translator, in theLost Children Archive,she’s a sound documentarist. And in theBeginning Middle End, she’s a fiction writer.

The narrator somehow has grown alongside me. You know, it’s like she’s a kind of presence in my life, as are her children, stepchildren, and half children. It’s sort of this lightly alternate world that communicates. Not so much with mine, but with my curiosities, with my pains, with my desire to understand things a little deeper.

I always end up writing about what I don’t know when I start writing a book, and the process of writing it is a process of me trying to get closer to knowing something. It’s the process of inquiry and research, deep essaying, trying things out, and there are always things left unexplored or not explored to the depth at which I would have liked to explore them. There’s always a moment in a novel when you have to abandon a path because you are already on another. Those abandoned paths are ones that I often pick up again in another book.

OM: One of the narrative forms you use in this book is sound, something you’ve also explored in your previous work. Can you talk about that choice and what drew you to it?

title: 3 Debut Authors Discuss How to Live in the Hypothetical
desc: For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One ma...
content:
For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One may argue that all fiction is rooted in imaginary lives, but these novels especially feel centered around thestakesof these imaginary lives as the protagonists confront, examine, wonder, and muse upon each of their choice’s ramifications on the rest of their years. From the gritty-and-glamorous art scene of Manhattan to the humid teenage June of northeastern Ohio to a suburban, emergency-laden town in Massachusetts, these three novels feature forks in the road and irreversible decisions that fall like dominoes upon characters and their next chapters.

“It was strange to see John in the studio, completely at a loss as to how to move his body, unsure of how to orient himself toward art.” So beginsGood Newsby Alexa Yasemin Brahme, a novel centered on Maggie, a Turkish-American MFA student finalizing her evocative thesis painting of “feminine suffering” while competing with her brother’s girlfriend, who has given herself the moniker of “the Artist.” Set in the contemporary New York art scene, the novel follows Maggie as she tries to orient herself within a branching future. Through gallery openings, social climbing parties, doubts about her boyfriend, and the return of an enigmatic ex, Maggie is forced to decide which life or alternate life she’ll end up choosing. In this world, a vertical brushstroke can change the entire canvas, and one phone call can upend everything she’s built.Good Newsinvites it all, plus the chaos, pleasure, and temptation of being young—that is, of creating worlds that leak out of our heads.

“Growing up, I had two best friends—Margaret, whom I had known my whole life, and Eleanor, with whom I was in love, though for years I had no reason to tell my feelings for one apart from my feelings for the other.” InGirl’s Girlby Sonia Feldman—set in that long summer between freshman and sophomore year of high school—Mina is caught in a web of desire, both platonic and erotic. It is a novel about living in suburban Ohio and creating those “capital E Experiences” that stay with you long after graduation. Reading it, I could almost smell the chlorine of untouched pools and that sticky perfume of bug spray sweating off skin at the end of the night. The messiness of the Midwest summer and unrequited love and dazzling adolescent confessions run rampant in this debut.

“Beckitt’s emergency began on a calm spring morning: an expansive chill in the air; the sun soaring over rangy, adolescent clouds; miles of rolling green mowed into submission, flanked by grand columns of oak and maple, through which the wind shivered.” When a ballistic missile alert threatens the town of Beckitt on a mundane morning, the town and its cast of characters are confronted with that most human decision: fight-or-flight. But when the second alert comes in, claiming that the first was a false alarm, the real decisions become clear. Where does one go from here? What did each person choose to save or leave behind? And how will these ramifications infiltrate the rest of their lives and those surrounding them?Seek Immediate Shelterby Vincent Yu explores the question of “what if” at its zenith. The novel follows five different characters and moves through each of their perspectives when the alert was sent, and then the aftermath, which for some may prove to be an even more daunting emergency than that initial missile threat.

Brahme, Feldman, and Yu corresponded with me on the significance of perspective in their novels, the spark that ignited and transformed their hypothetical questions into fiction, and the advice they would impart to anyone becoming a debut novelist.

Kyla D Walker: Did you know right away that the book would be from Maggie’s third-person limited POV, or did you consider a first-person POV as well? What ultimately led you to choose third-person narration, and how did this change the novel’s approach?

Alexa Yasemin Brahme:First person is an intimidating point of view—“I” can be very powerful. First person felt immediate, intimate, and had a sure-footedness that wasn’t quite right for Maggie. The first person feels to me like certainty. We readers are getting the account straight from the source, and when that source is unreliable, like I think Maggie would be, the first person feels like a slight of hand a character is performing against the reader. What’s presented as fact is actually distorted. I wanted there to be a little distance between the reader and Maggie so she couldn’t hide from their gaze. Maggie can’t present her take on the situation because the reader can see multiple sides at once. While Maggie can trick herself into believing one version of the story, she can’t trick the reader.

That said, when I was drafting and editing the book, if I got stuck in certain scenes wondering what Maggie would say or do, I would write them in first person to see if there was anything Maggie could reveal to me about herself. If it proved to be useful, I’d take what I’d written and massage it into a third-person version for the final draft.

First person is an intimidating point of view—’I’ can be very powerful.

KDW: I love Maggie’s thesis painting and all it represents, and I’m so curious about its conception. Did the painting’s concept—the image of multiple women in mundane settings yet extreme pain—come before the novel, or did it arise through the novel’s writing and Maggie’s character?

AYB:The painting was challenging for me to conceive of while I was writing the book. Turns out, not being a visual artist is a huge impairment to writing about visual art. When I started working on the novel, I had no idea what the painting would depict. I knew I wanted the subject of the work to be about women and their particular plight in this world. And it wasn’t crucial, at least to me, that the painting be perfectly visible throughout the book. My main concerns were the feelings surrounding the art. At times, the painting feels bleak and depressing, and later in the book, Maggie realizes its greater meaning is deeper than just “Women Suffer.”

Strangely, writing the painting felt like a process Maggie and I were constructing together. It feels likewefigured it out, which makesmesound absolutely insane.

title: Finding Your Voice as a Woman Writer Raised on Books by Men
desc: Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently ...
content:
Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently become Electric Literature’s Executive Director. I was an aspiring writer with a few short stories; Julie was about to publish her debut novel,Marlena, to critical and commercial acclaim. We hit it off as two hard-working, mostly type-A people with the same cynical sense of humor that protects over-eager emotions, and began trading work after we both left the city. Julie to Ann Arbor where she was teaching at the University of Michigan and writing her sophomore novel,Famous Men; me to upstate New York where I was working on my debut novel,Slush, which will be published next summer. Julie is my most trusted reader. I have long felt like I can say anything to her; that nothing is too strange, or dark, or vulnerable, or naïve. If I am working out a difficult opinion, she can help me articulate it. What better qualities to have in a writing partner?

Famous Mentells the story of Wilhelmina Miles, known as Will, an aspiring poet from the small town of Greening, Michigan. She has long harbored the fantasy that her town’s one success story, the decorated writer Nathanial Fellow, is her father. When she moves to New York and tracks him down at the MFA program where he teaches, that fantasy deforms into a relationship, one that is financial, professional, sexual, and even a little familial.

Famous Menis an entertaining, rich, discomfiting novel that rejects black and white answers to complex questions in favor of subjectivity as its foundational stance. Consent is not a matter of “yes” or “no,” culpability is not an easy verdict, and power is multi-directional.

Reading early drafts ofFamous Men, I was struck by how they never quite felt like drafts. Scenes were cut, plot points changed, etc., but the world of the novel and the ideas behind it always felt fully formed. Julie has a charismatic prose style that is flowing yet precise, with a clarity of insight that seems casual but is most certainly hard won. When the galley finally arrived, I thought I would dip in and out to gather questions for this interview. But I couldn’t resist reading straight through for a third time; the novel is that compelling and rewarding.

Julie and I spoke over video call, with some follow-up over email. I found myself surprisingly nervous to ask her “serious questions” on the record, after so many casual, private conversations. Initial giggling aside, we settled in, and I was grateful to be able to engage with her not as my friend, but as the author of one of my favorite books of this decade.

Halimah Marcus: Will, long before she ever meets Nathaniel, reads his work at the library. And because they’re from the same small town, it sparks her imagination about what she could be someday. Who were the writers that did that for you when you were that age?

Julie Buntin:I grew up in Hemingway country. I grew up in the Petoskey area of Northern Michigan where the Nick Adams stories on Walloon Lake are set. Hemingway lived in a lot of places, but there’s a lot of regional Hemingway pride where I’m from in a way I took for granted as a young person—that a small town like that might celebrate their literary grandfather out of pride. My husband’s family is from Lorain, Ohio, where Toni Morrison is from, and he went looking for her house once. There was nothing that said Toni Morrison lived there.

Hemingway was a writer I liked and read at a young age because we had his books in our house,The Sun Also Rises,For Whom the Bell Tolls, obviously the stories. I wasn’t necessarily thinking,I want to write like this, but I did have this idea of certain writers as having this cultural impact. I also read a ton of Stephen King, like so much Stephen King.

HM: Will internalizes a lot of lessons from being so obsessed with Nathaniel’s work. There’s this great passage about all the women in Nathaniel’s fiction, and the limits of who they could be and the archetypes they represent. Did you internalize any lessons like that from your reading as a young person?

JB:With this book, I wrestled a lot with questions I still sit with. I remember readingHerzogby Saul Bellow as a teenager and thinking:This is genius. The high/low voice; it’s so funny. How does he do this? This is everything I could ever want to do as a writer.And then having a similar reaction to theRabbit, Runnovels by John Updike, loving them without any ability at that age to question the complicated portrayals of women, which are sometimes really reductive.

In this book, I was thinking a lot about what happens if part of your formative artistic development involves taking in influences that don’t always make space for your full subjectivity as a person. What happens if those are the models you put ahead of everything else? If the first character you identify with in serious literature is like, a middle-aged man? I was thinking about not only how that would affect you as a writer, but how it would affect your sense of what kind of woman you wanted to be or could be.

We’re so permeable to influence when we’re children and adolescents, especially. I see this with my son, who is five—he reads something and suddenly he’s repeating phrases from it, acting like the characters. That’s something I’m endlessly interested in, so that was floating around in my head for sure: How might there be bleeding between what Will reads and what she thinks? How she presents herself to Nathaniel, how she understands how he might see her—all of that is a creation of her imagination, but also created by the texts of his that she’s read.
